title: Module Header: Roth Number and Three-Part Structure
content: The file opens with a documentation block introducing the Roth number $r_3(N)$ — the maximum size of a 3-AP-free subset of $\{0, \ldots, N-1\}$ — and outlines the three-part structure: definitions (Part I), density increment iteration (Part II), and quantitative bound statements (Part III). The single `import Mathlib` pulls in the full Mathlib library, providing ZMod, Finset, Real.log, Real.exp, and the positivity/omega tactics. The file uses the `open Finset` command to bring Finset operations into scope without qualification, and works within the namespace `Szemeredi.Roth.Quantitative`, reflecting that Roth's theorem is the $k=3$ case of Szemerédi's theorem on arithmetic progressions.
mathContext: The Roth number $r_3(N) = \max\{|A| : A \subseteq [N],\, A \text{ has no 3-AP}\}$ quantifies how dense a set can be while avoiding 3-term arithmetic progressions. This file works in $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ rather than $[N]$ for algebraic convenience.

title: AP-Free Sets in ZMod N
content: Defines the core predicate: a set A ⊆ ℤ/Nℤ is AP-free if it contains no 3-term arithmetic progression a, a+d, a+2d with d ≠ 0. Working in ZMod N (cyclic group) rather than {1,...,N} simplifies the group structure and allows direct application of Fourier/spectral methods. The condition d ≠ 0 excludes the trivial case where all three terms coincide.
mathContext: $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ is AP-free if: $\forall a, d \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z},\; d \neq 0 \Rightarrow a \in A \Rightarrow a+d \in A \Rightarrow a+2d \notin A$

title: The Roth Number r₃(N)
content: The Roth number r₃(N) is defined as the supremum of |A| over all AP-free subsets A of ZMod N, implemented via Finset.sup. The definition is `noncomputable` because taking a supremum over a powerset of a finite type is logically definable but not algorithmically extractable in Lean. The note about N=0 (where ZMod 0 = ℤ is infinite) shows careful attention to edge cases at the boundary of the definition's domain.

title: Basic AP-Free Properties: Empty, Singleton, Subset
content: Three foundational lemmas about the APFree predicate. The empty set proof uses absurdity from membership in ∅. The singleton proof is the most interesting: it shows that in a singleton {x}, having a, a+d both in {x} forces a = x and a+d = x, which gives d = 0, contradicting the hypothesis. The subset lemma follows directly by chasing hypotheses through the monotone predicate. These form the essential toolkit for constructing AP-free witnesses.

title: The Full Set Is Never AP-Free (N ≥ 2)
content: For N ≥ 2, the elements 0, 1, 2 form a 3-AP in ZMod N (with a=0, d=1). This theorem uses Lean's `Fact` typeclass mechanism to activate the hypothesis 1 < N inside the proof. The approach is direct: exhibit the AP {0, 1, 2} and apply the APFree hypothesis to derive a contradiction. This is the key fact that forces r₃(N) < N for N ≥ 2.
mathContext: In $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ with $N \geq 2$: the progression $0, 1, 2$ (with $a=0, d=1$) is a 3-AP, so $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ itself is not AP-free.

title: Basic Quantitative Bounds on r₃(N)
content: Four theorems establish the trivial bounds: r₃(N) ≤ N (since AP-free sets are subsets), r₃(N) < N for N ≥ 2 (since univ is not AP-free), r₃(N) ≤ N-1 (corollary), and 1 ≤ r₃(N) (singleton witness). The proof of rothNumber_lt is noteworthy: it uses Finset.sup_lt_iff, then a cardinality squeeze showing any AP-free set of full size equals univ, contradicting not_apFree_univ. The positivity proof exhibits {0} as a concrete AP-free witness and uses Finset.le_sup.
mathContext: For $N \geq 1$: $1 \leq r_3(N) \leq N-1$ when $N \geq 2$, and $r_3(1) = 1$. The lower bound comes from the singleton $\{0\}$; the upper bound from $\text{APFree}(A) \Rightarrow A \neq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$.

title: Any AP-Free Set Is Bounded by r₃(N)
content: Proves the fundamental characterization of the Roth number as a true upper bound: for any AP-free subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$, we have $|A| \leq r_3(N)$. The proof unfolds the Roth number definition and applies `Finset.le_sup` to show that $A$'s cardinality is at most the supremum over all AP-free sets. This theorem is the workhorse used to establish upper bounds on $r_3(N)$: to prove $r_3(N) \leq f(N)$, it suffices to show that every AP-free set has cardinality at most $f(N)$. Combined with `rothNumber_achieved`, this gives a complete characterization: $r_3(N)$ is the exact maximum, not merely a least upper bound.
mathContext: $\forall A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z},\; \text{APFree}(A) \Rightarrow |A| \leq r_3(N)$. Proof: $A$ belongs to the set $\{B \in 2^{\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}} : \text{APFree}(B)\}$, so $|A| \leq \sup_B |B| = r_3(N)$.

title: The Maximum Is Achieved: Compactness for Finite Sets
content: Proves that r₃(N) is not merely a supremum but an actual maximum — there exists an AP-free set A with |A| = r₃(N). The proof uses Finset.exists_max_image, which is a finite version of the extreme value theorem: any nonempty finite set has a maximum element under any function. This is automatic for finite sets but requires explicit proof in Lean. The witness set S of all AP-free subsets is nonempty (it contains ∅), allowing the maximum to be extracted.
mathContext: $\exists A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}: \text{APFree}(A) \wedge |A| = r_3(N)$. This follows from finiteness of $2^{\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}}$, unlike the analogous statement for infinite sets where compactness is needed.

title: Exact Values: r₃(2) = 1 and r₃(3) = 2
content: Computes the Roth number for the two smallest meaningful cases. For r₃(2)=1: the bounds give 1 ≤ r₃(2) < 2, so r₃(2)=1 by omega. For r₃(3)=2: the set {0,1} in ZMod 3 is AP-free (verified by fin_cases, exhaustively checking all elements and differences), giving 2 ≤ r₃(3). Combined with r₃(3) < 3, this pins down r₃(3)=2. The fin_cases + simp_all tactic combination handles the finite case analysis automatically.
mathContext: $r_3(2) = 1$: only singletons are AP-free in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. $r_3(3) = 2$: $\{0,1\}$ is maximal AP-free in $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ (note $\{0,1,2\}$ contains the AP $0,1,2$).

title: Density Increment: Iteration Count Bound
content: The heart of the density increment method, formalized. If an AP-free set has density δ, the density increment argument produces a substructure with density δ + δ²/100. The theorem proves this process terminates: after more than ⌊100/δ²⌋ steps, the density would exceed 1. The proof uses Nat.floor_le to bound the floor function and a chain of inequalities to derive the contradiction. This is one of the few fully proved (no sorry) theorems in Part II.
mathContext: If density increases as $\delta_k = \delta_0 + k\delta_0^2/100$, then $\delta_k > 1$ forces $k > \lfloor 100/\delta_0^2 \rfloor$. Equivalently: at most $\lfloor 100/\delta^2 \rfloor$ density increments are possible before reaching density 1.

title: Iteration Contrapositive and the Modulus Decay Obstacle
content:
The `iterations_before_contradiction` theorem provides the contrapositive of `max_iterations_bound`: if density $\delta + k\delta^2/100 \leq 1$, then $(k : \mathbb{R}) \leq 100/\delta^2$. This is the form directly used in quantitative arguments — one shows that the density stays at most 1 after $k$ steps, then deduces a bound on $k$.

The NOTE comment (lines 169–174) documents a critical correction: the previously stated `density_upper_bound_from_iteration` (claiming $r_3(N) \leq 10\sqrt{N}$) was **false** for large $N$. Behrend's lower bound gives $r_3(N) \geq N \cdot \exp(-c\sqrt{\log N}) \gg \sqrt{N}$. The error arose from assuming the density increment gives a substructure of size $M$ with $M \geq N^c$, when in fact the increment lemma only guarantees $M < N$ with no lower bound. This gap is the precise obstacle to completing Roth's quantitative argument formally: one needs Fourier-analytic estimates (Roth's $M \geq N^{2/3}$) to control the modulus decay rate.
mathContext: Contrapositive: $\delta + k\delta^2/100 \leq 1 \Rightarrow k \leq 100/\delta^2$. The false claim $r_3(N) \leq 10\sqrt{N}$ was refuted by Behrend: $r_3(N) \geq N \cdot e^{-c\sqrt{\log N}} \gg N^{1-\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon > 0$.

title: The Key Obstacle: Modulus Decay Rate
content: The sorry in density_upper_bound_from_iteration identifies the precise mathematical obstacle to completing Roth's proof: the density increment lemma (from RothTheorem.lean) gives a substructure of size M < N but with no lower bound on M. For quantitative bounds, one needs M ≥ N^c (Roth uses M ≥ N^{2/3}) to control how fast N decreases across iterations. Without this lower bound, one cannot count the number of iterations or extract a quantitative bound on δ.
mathContext: The blocked step: given $\delta N \leq r_3(N)$, density increment gives AP-free set in $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$ with density $\delta + \delta^2/100$, but need $M \geq N^c$ to bound iteration count. Roth shows $M \geq N^{2/3}$, giving $\leq \log_{3/2}(\log N)$ iterations.

title: Roth's 1953 Bound: r₃(N) ≤ CN/log(log N)
content: States Roth's original quantitative bound from his 1953 paper. The proof sketch (in the docstring) shows the strategy: density increment with M ≥ N^{2/3} at each step gives at most log_{3/2}(log N) iterations before modulus reaches O(1), forcing δ ≤ C/√(log log N). Roth's more refined analysis (tracking M ≥ N^{2/3} carefully) improves this to δ ≤ C/log(log N). This bound stood as the best known result for nearly 50 years before Bourgain's improvements.
mathContext: $r_3(N) \leq C \cdot \frac{N}{\log\log N}$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$. Equivalently: any $A \subseteq [N]$ with $|A| \geq C'N/\log\log N$ contains a 3-term AP.

title: Behrend's 1946 Construction: Near-Optimal Lower Bound
content: Behrend's construction (predating Roth's upper bound!) produces large AP-free sets. The key idea: take lattice points on a d-dimensional sphere of radius R. Points on a sphere form an AP a, b, c only if a=b=c (since ‖a‖²+‖c‖²=2‖b‖² and ‖a‖=‖b‖=‖c‖ implies a=b=c). Project these sphere points into ZMod N via a suitable injection. Optimizing d and R gives sets of size N·exp(-c√(log N)), beating any polynomial improvement over Roth. This lower bound has remained essentially best-known for 80 years.
mathContext: $r_3(N) \geq N \cdot \exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})$ for some $c > 0$. The construction uses $d$-dimensional spheres with $d \approx \sqrt{\log N}$, containing $\approx N^{1-c/\sqrt{\log N}}$ lattice points that project injectively into $[N]$.

title: Bloom-Sisask (2020): Breaking the Logarithmic Barrier
content: For decades, improvements to Roth's bound stalled around N/(log N)^{1-ε}. Bloom and Sisask broke through to N/(log N)^{1+c}, the first time any power of log N greater than 1 appeared in the denominator. Their approach used a quantitative version of the Bogolyubov lemma and a more careful analysis of Bohr sets, obtaining density increments on structured sets that are much larger than those in Roth's original argument. This was a major conceptual breakthrough foreshadowing Kelley-Meka.
mathContext: $r_3(N) \leq \frac{N}{(\log N)^{1+c}}$ for some absolute $c > 0$. Prior best: Bourgain (1999) $N/(\log N)^{1-\varepsilon}$, Sanders (2011) $N\log\log N/(\log N)$.

title: Kelley-Meka (2023): Near-Behrend Upper Bound
content: The 2023 breakthrough by Kelley and Meka achieved r₃(N) ≤ N·exp(-c(log N)^{1/12}), coming closer to Behrend's lower bound than any previous result. Their key innovation was a density increment argument on Bohr sets with improved spectral structure, using polynomial methods and higher-order Fourier analysis. The gap between the upper bound exp(-c(log N)^{1/12}) and the lower bound exp(-c√(log N)) remains open — the exponent 1/12 vs 1/2 is a fundamental barrier. The Kelley-Meka proof appeared on arXiv in February 2023 and was verified correct within weeks.
mathContext: $r_3(N) \leq N \cdot \exp(-c(\log N)^{1/12})$. Compare with Behrend lower bound: $r_3(N) \geq N \cdot \exp(-c'\sqrt{\log N})$. The exponents $1/12$ vs $1/2$ represent the remaining gap.
